narrative:
Your predicted probability of failing the bar exam on the first try was 56%, meaning the model judged failure slightly more likely than success. Because your application was screened on that risk, it was denied.

The decisive factor was your third-year class standing. You are in the first decile, whereas accepted students average around the sixth decile; this very low relative standing pushed the prediction most strongly toward bar-exam failure. Your first-year standing was the second-most influential factor: at the fourth decile, below the accepted average of about the sixth, it nevertheless counted modestly toward passing and did not outweigh the third-year concern. Your undergraduate GPA of 2.40, compared with an accepted-student average of 3.23, was the third-most influential factor and also leaned slightly toward passing in the model’s assessment, but it was not enough to change the overall result. Your LSAT score of 30, below the accepted average of about 37, was not among the three strongest signals but still illustrates the academic-risk profile.

To improve a future application, focus first on demonstrating stronger upper-level academic performance and seek advising on a realistic bar-exam preparation plan. Consider LSAT preparation or retaking the exam, additional coursework or a post-baccalaureate program to raise your GPA, and ask admissions for feedback. Reapply only after you can show new evidence of readiness.
